segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Avot's forty-eight: say who said it. Today a new block opens, and it's full of names said in the name of names.

segments.voice: A box set of a show you've never watched, dozens of episodes, and a friend says: start at the beginning, no skipping. A tractate of Talmud asks the same thing. This block reads one, Berakhot, the tractate of blessings, from its first page to its last. Slowly, a little each day, the way a long show gets watched. And its first page is numbered two.
screen: `START AT THE BEGINNING.` → `NO SKIPPING.` → `PAGE ONE IS PAGE TWO.`

segments.voice: The word is masechet, a tractate: one book of the Talmud, on one subject. The same Hebrew word names the woven web in the story of Samson, cloth on a loom, and some readers hear that in it: a tractate is woven, threads of voices crossing. Pick up a printed volume and your senses tell you the rest. It's heavy. It smells like old paper. On each page, a block of text sits in the middle, the Mishnah and its discussion, with smaller commentaries wrapped around it. And it opens on page two, side a. Berakhot's first question isn't about God or belief. It's about the clock. From when do we recite the Shema in the evening? The Mishnah answers: from the hour the priests go in to eat their holy portion, until the end of the first watch, says Rabbi Eliezer. The sages say, until midnight. Rabban Gamaliel says, until dawn. Three answers on the first page, and nobody is erased. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: Berakhot opens with an argument about bedtime. That's why this block reads in order. Skip around and you collect quotes. Read one tractate start to finish and you hear a conversation: threads coming back, names you'll meet again. Berakhot is about blessings, the Shema, prayer, words over food, and for the next weeks it's ours, page by page.
screen: `MASECHET: ONE WOVEN BOOK.` · `HEAVY, OLD PAPER, PAGE TWO.` · `FIRST QUESTION: WHEN IS EVENING?` · `THREE ANSWERS, NONE ERASED.` · then, large: `A TRACTATE IS WOVEN: READ IT IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Find something woven near you: a sleeve, a scarf, a towel, the spine of a book. Run a fingertip slowly along it and feel where the threads cross. Let that be the picture for the sit: many threads, one piece, held together by going in order.
Masechet. A tractate: one book of the Talmud on one subject. The same word names a woven web.
Hold onto this one: a tractate is woven, so read it in order, no skipping ahead. Berakhot, day one of fifty.

howItsDone: Many Jews learn Talmud a page at a time, in order, often with a study partner or in a daily class; finishing a whole tractate is marked with a siyum, a small celebration.
